title: Behar: wronging with words (Leviticus 25:17)
hookLine: the rabbis read "ye shall not wrong one another" as a ban on hurtful words (Bava Metzia 58b)
tomorrow: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)

cards: A man walks into a pottery shop with no plan to buy anything. He picks up a bowl, turns it over, and asks the owner, how much for this one? Her face lights up.
She names a price, starts wrapping it, mentions she made the glaze herself. He shrugs, puts it down, and leaves. Nothing was stolen.
Not a coin changed hands. And yet the Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code, lists exactly this moment as a wrong.

teach.b: Leviticus twenty-five says it twice. Verse fourteen, about buying and selling: don't wrong one another. Then verse seventeen: "And ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God; for I am the LORD your God."
The rabbis noticed the repeat. Money was already covered, so, the Talmud says in Bava Metzia fifty-eight b, the second verse must be about words.
They called it ona'at devarim, wronging with words. Ona'ah is cheating someone on a price; devarim means words. The Mishnah's examples are startlingly specific.
Don't ask the price of something you have no intention of buying: you're raising hope you'll dash. If someone has turned their life around, don't say, remember what you used to do.
A teaching quoted in the Talmud adds: if someone is suffering, don't lecture them that they must have earned it, the way Job's friends did. Then the Talmud goes further.
Embarrassing someone in public is like shedding blood: you can watch the color drain from their face.
It argues that wronging with words is worse than wronging with money, and one reason is simple. Money can be paid back.

teach.h: YE SHALL NOT WRONG ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: A word, once it lands, can't be collected. And the verse closes with fear thy God, the same ending that came with the stumbling block. Here it lands on speech.
A remark can be passed off as a joke, and only the speaker knows whether it was meant as a knife.

how: Jewish ethical teaching treats hurtful speech as a serious wrong; the laws of ona'at devarim, from Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 and the Talmud's discussion at 58b, are studied alongside the laws of gossip, and public embarrassment is treated as a grave harm.

o: cheating someone on the price of goods
wronging with words: hurting someone's dignity
breaking a promise you made out loud

games.q: wronging with words — tap the pairs.

s: the Mishnah counts asking a price you won't pay as a wrong
it raises the seller's hope for nothing.
the rabbis said hurtful words matter less than cheating on money
the Talmud calls words worse: money can be repaid, words can't.
reminding a person who changed of their old ways is fine if it's true
the Mishnah names it as wronging with words.

games.q: you're browsing a shop with no plan to buy. you like a bowl. what does the Mishnah say about asking its price?
o: don't ask if you have no intention of buying.
ask, but only on a quiet day.
games.why: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 lists it as ona'at devarim: you raise the seller's hope with no plan to fulfill it.

practice: Think back over the last day or two to a moment when a sharp line rose up in you: a reply to a text, a comment about someone's cooking, a joke at a sibling's expense.
Replay it slowly, and notice the tiny gap between thinking the words and saying them. Rest there for a few breaths; that gap is where today's verse lives.

wordCard.voice: Ona'at devarim. Wronging with words: cheating someone of their dignity the way a bad merchant cheats them of money.

orig.note: Hebrew: wronging with words. ona'ah is overcharging; devarim, words.

carryVoice: Your line: words can wrong. The gap before speaking is yours to keep. That's day four hundred twenty-three.
